request.system:
You assist an automated astronomer who infers how a body moves from angles-only sky observations (ecliptic longitude/latitude seen from an observer whose orbit is known). Jan, the fitting engine, fits candidate model families by least squares and compares them by Bayesian evidence. You see numerical summaries of the current best fit and its residuals, and you propose the next candidates to fit.

A candidate is either a registered family (by exact name) or a new central force law: the radial acceleration f(r) in AU/day^2 (negative = attractive) as an expression in r (heliocentric distance, AU), GM (the Sun's, 2.959e-4 AU^3/day^2, fixed) and parameters you declare with bounds and an initial value. Allowed in expressions: numbers, + - * / **, parentheses, exp, log, sqrt, tanh, pi, r, GM and your parameter names (lowercase, letters/digits/underscore). Prefer the simplest law that explains the residual structure; a new parameter must buy a clear improvement. Reply "stop": true when the residuals are consistent with noise or further candidates are unlikely to help.

parsed.analysis: Every model fits very poorly. The fitted noise is about 162,000 arcsec (roughly 45°), and the residual rms is about 85°. The residuals by time show large, non-monotonic means. The two half-span ellipse fits disagree badly: periods of 860 and 600 days, with about 17°/orbit apsidal motion. Both periods are much shorter than the Keplerian value for a~3.1 AU (about 2000 days). This points to a strong secular or time-dependent perturbation, or a mis-specified geometry, rather than a simple radial-law tweak. The free power law (n≈2.16, C>GM) beats Newton only because it can absorb a stronger effective attraction plus precession. Three directions remain untested. First, an unseen perturbing planet, which gives period changes and precession. Second, a Yukawa-type deviation. Third, a Newton term with free strength plus a Hooke-like term, which gives shorter periods and apsidal motion with smooth radial structure. Residuals are clearly not noise-consistent, so I will not stop.

proposals.rationale: A large unseen perturber can change the apparent period between halves and drive apsidal motion (~17°/orbit). These effects cannot be captured by any static central law fitted so far.

The free strength k allows the shorter-than-Keplerian period implied by the fit (C>GM). The linear term adds a distinct radial dependence that produces apsidal precession. This separates scaling and precession more cleanly than a single power index.
This is a registered alternative central deviation not yet tested. It is a cheap check of whether a distance-dependent screening explains the radial-bin structure.
